Marburg Colloquy
MAR-burg KOL-uh-kwee
noun (church history)
From Marburg, the German town where Philip of Hesse convened the conference in 1529, + colloquy (Latin colloquium, a speaking together); the meeting of Luther and Zwingli over the Lord's Supper.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Marburg Colloquy of 1529 was the conference at which Philip of Hesse sought to unite the German and Swiss Reformations by reconciling Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli. The two streams agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles — the Trinity, the person of Christ, justification by faith, the rejection of the Mass as sacrifice — and broke over the fifteenth: the nature of Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper. Luther held to a bodily presence in, with, and under the bread, chalking on the table the words Hoc est corpus meum, "This is my body," and refusing every figurative reading. Zwingli argued that "is" means "signifies," that Christ's body is at the Father's right hand and cannot be bodily in the bread, and that the Supper is a memorial sign received by faith. At the parting Luther would not grant Zwingli the hand of fellowship, saying they were of a different spirit. The breach was never healed in their lifetimes, and it left the Reformation divided into Lutheran and Reformed. This dictionary, holding the Reformed position, judges Zwingli the nearer to the truth on the letter while owning Calvin's later refinement — a real spiritual feeding on Christ by faith — as the fullest biblical account.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The 1529 conference where Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen articles but split on the Lord's Supper — Luther holding a bodily presence, Zwingli a memorial received by faith. The breach divided the Reformation into Lutheran and Reformed.

expand to see more

MARBURG COLLOQUY, noun. The 1529 conference at Marburg, convened by Philip of Hesse, between Luther and Zwingli.

Agreement was reached on fourteen of fifteen articles of doctrine.

The split came on the fifteenth: the manner of Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper.

Luther insisted on a bodily presence ("This is my body"); Zwingli on a memorial sign received by faith.

The breach was not healed; it divided the Reformation into Lutheran and Reformed streams.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Cor 11:24 — "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

John 6:63 — "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."

Acts 3:21 — "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things."

1 Cor 10:16 — "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The modern temptation is to call the Marburg breach a sad squabble over words and to wish the Reformers had simply agreed to differ — as though the real presence of Christ in His own ordinance were a matter of indifference rather than of truth.

expand to see more

Ecumenical readers treat Marburg as a cautionary tale of stubbornness: if only Luther had unbent, the Protestant house would not have divided. But the question was not trivial. Whether Christ's true body is locally present in the bread touches His humanity, His ascension, and the meaning of His own words. Luther rightly refused to let "is my body" be emptied of all force; Zwingli rightly refused a carnal presence that denies Christ's bodily session at the Father's right hand (Acts 3:21). The dictionary will not flatten that into a misunderstanding over semantics.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but it does meet the modern instinct to prize unity above truth. The principle to recover is that doctrine matters even when it costs fellowship, and that the Lord's Supper is no small thing to err in. Calvin's mature teaching — that believers truly feed on the body and blood of Christ spiritually, by the Holy Spirit and through faith, while Christ remains bodily in heaven — is the dictionary's answer to both errors, and the position the 1689 Confession carries.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Marburg (the town) + Latin colloquium (a speaking together); the 1529 debate over the words of institution, "This is my body."

expand to see more

Marburg — the Hessian town where Philip of Hesse hosted the conference

Latin colloquium, a conference or speaking together

The point of rupture: Hoc est corpus meum, "This is my body" (1 Cor 11:24)

Lutheran reading: bodily presence in, with, and under the bread

Reformed reading: a memorial sign with a true spiritual feeding by faith

Usage

"At the Marburg Colloquy the Reformation agreed on fourteen articles and divided over one."

"Luther chalked "This is my body" on the Marburg table and would not yield the figurative sense."

"The Marburg Colloquy left a wound between Lutheran and Reformed that Calvin labored to heal."
